claim: Human T cells have a stiffness in the range of 0.1 kPa.
source: Human T cells are extremely soft, in the range of 0.1 kPa (Bufi et al., 2015; Guillou et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bufi et al., 2015; Guillou et al., 2016).

claim: Skeletal muscle stiffness is in the range of tens of kPa.
source: skeletal muscle stiffness is in the range of tens of kPa (Uffmann et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Uffmann et al., 2004).

claim: Calcified bone can reach stiffness values of GPa.
source: calcified bone can reach values of GPa (Gasiorowski et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gasiorowski et al., 2013).

claim: Stiffness influences cell growth, differentiation, migration and survival for many cell types.
source: For many cell types, stiffness has been shown to influence cell growth, differentiation, migration and survival (Pelham and Wang, 1997; Lo et al., 2000; Discher et al., 2005; Engler et al., 2006; Solon et al., 2007; Oakes et al., 2009; Trappmann et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Substrate stiffness affects T cell activation.
source: In T cells, substrate stiffness was shown to affect T cell activation (Judokusumo et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2012; Tabdanov et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Judokusumo et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2012; Tabdanov et al., 2015).

claim: Substrate stiffness regulates the forces exerted by T cells on their substrates.
source: In T cells, substrate stiffness was shown to affect T cell activation (Judokusumo et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2012; Tabdanov et al., 2015) and to regulate the forces exerted by T cells on their substrates (Husson et al., 2011; Hui et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Husson et al., 2011; Hui et al., 2015).

claim: Stiffness regulates the cytotoxicity of T lymphocytes.
source: Moreover, it was also recently proposed to regulate the cytotoxicity of T lymphocytes (Basu et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Basu et al., 2016).

claim: The stiffness of myeloid APCs ranges from 0.2 to 1.5 kPa.
source: However, most studies, especially for CD4+ T cells, were looking into a handful of parameters and/or used a stiffness range that did not take into account the stiffness of myeloid APCs (0.2 to 1.5 kPa), which was shown to vary according to APC type and inflammatory conditions (Bufi et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bufi et al., 2015).

claim: Migration, gene expression, cytokine secretion, metabolism and cell cycle progression of human CD4+ T lymphocytes are affected by stiffness of the activating substrates.
source: Our results show that migration, gene expression, cytokine secretion, metabolism and cell cycle progression of human CD4+ T lymphocytes are affected by stiffness of the activating substrates.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including migration assays, gene expression analysis, cytokine measurements, metabolic assays, and cell cycle analysis.

claim: Some T cell functions are sensitive to potentiation from a low rigidity range (in the order of magnitude reported for APC), while others are mostly affected by higher rigidity (in the order of magnitude reported for tissues).
source: They also reveal that some functions are sensitive to this potentiation from a low rigidity range (in the order of magnitude reported for APC), while others are mostly affected by higher rigidity (in the order of magnitude reported for tissues).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing differential sensitivity of various T cell functions to different stiffness ranges.

claim: Human CD4+ T cells can modulate their responses according to their mechanical environment.
source: Therefore, human CD4+ T cells can modulate their responses according to their mechanical environment, with the TCR being an exquisite mechanosensor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that T cells respond differently to varying substrate stiffness.

claim: The TCR is an exquisite mechanosensor.
source: Therefore, human CD4+ T cells can modulate their responses according to their mechanical environment, with the TCR being an exquisite mechanosensor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing TCR-dependent responses to substrate stiffness and by citations to previous research on TCR mechanosensing.

claim: The mean instantaneous velocity of migrating T cells on ICAM-1 coated PA-gels is significantly higher for the stiff 100 kPa gel (15.5 ± 0.4 μm/min) than for the 0.5 kPa (12.4 ± 0.3 μm/min) and 6.4 kPa gel (13.1 ± 0.3 μm/min).
source: For ICAM-1 coated PA-gels, the mean instantaneous velocity of migrating T cells (Figure 1A) was significantly but modestly higher for the stiff 100 kPa gel (15.5 ± 0.4 μm/min) than for the 0.5 kPa (12.4 ± 0.3 μm/min) and 6.4 kPa gel (13.1 ± 0.3 μm/min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from migration assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: T cells migrate over longer distances on the 100 kPa gels than on the 0.5 kPa and 6.4 kPa gels.
source: Similarly, calculating the maximum distance covered by the T cells on the substrate after 5 min revealed that T cells migrated over longer distances on the 100 kPa gels than on the 0.5 kPa and 6.4 kPa gels (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from migration assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The percentage of arrested T cells in the presence of aCD3+aCD28 is higher on the stiff 100 kPa gels than on the softer ones.
source: The percentage of arrested T cells in the presence of aCD3+aCD28 was higher on the stiff 100 kPa gels than on the softer ones (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of arrested cells never reached the level obtained on glass coated with aCD3+aCD28+ICAM-1.
source: Yet, percentage of arrested cells never reached the level obtained on glass coated with aCD3+aCD28+ICAM-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing arrest on PA-gels versus glass.

claim: aCD3 coupled to 0.5 and 6.4 kPa did not induce any significant deceleration of lymphoblasts.
source: Moreover, aCD3 coupled to 0.5 and 6.4 kPa did not induce any significant deceleration of lymphoblasts, while it did induce deceleration of non-arrested lymphoblasts when coupled to 100 kPa gels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: aCD3 induced deceleration of non-arrested lymphoblasts when coupled to 100 kPa gels.
source: Moreover, aCD3 coupled to 0.5 and 6.4 kPa did not induce any significant deceleration of lymphoblasts, while it did induce deceleration of non-arrested lymphoblasts when coupled to 100 kPa gels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Softer gels (0.5 and 6.4 kPa) allow for minimal spreading of some T cell extensions, whereas the T cell body does not spread.
source: Softer gels (0.5 and 6.4 kPa) allowed for minimal spreading of some T cell extensions, whereas the T cell body did not spread.
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Contact with the stiffest gel (100 kPa) induces more pronounced spreading of cell extensions.
source: Contact with the stiffest gel (100 kPa) induced more pronounced spreading of cell extensions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Protrusions on 0.5 and 6.4 kPa gels are thin (100–200 nm).
source: Protrusions on 0.5 and 6.4 kPa gels were thin (100–200 nm).
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy measurements.

claim: On 100 kPa gels, protrusions are similarly thin until they reach the surface, where they spread.
source: On 100 kPa gels, protrusions were similarly thin until they reached the surface, where they spread.
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy observations.

claim: The structures observed on PA-gels are reminiscent of the invadosome/podosome-like protrusions (ILPs) reported during T cell scanning of activated endothelial cells.
source: These structures were reminiscent of the invadosome/podosome-like protrusions (ILPs) reported during T cell scanning of activated endothelial cells that have rigidities in the order of kPa (Sage et al., 2012; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with structures described in cited literature (Sage et al., 2012; Kumari et al., 2015).

claim: On glass, T cells are extensively spread, with all the ventral membrane forming a single thin lamellipodium.
source: On glass, T cells were extensively spread, with all the ventral membrane forming a single thin lamellipodium, as previously shown (Bunnell et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy observations and a citation to previous research (Bunnell et al., 2001).

claim: The 'fried egg' shape was neither observed when T cells interacted with substrates of physiological stiffness range nor when in contact with dendritic cells.
source: However, it is worth noting that the 'fried egg' shape, reported in most reviews as the classical morphology of a T cell forming a mature synapse, was neither observed when T cells interacted with substrates of physiological stiffness range (herein) nor when in contact with dendritic cells (Trautmann and Valitutti, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental observations in this study and a citation to previous research (Trautmann and Valitutti, 2003).

claim: Within a physiological stiffness range, T cells scan their substrate through thin protrusions but do not spread extensively their cell body in response to TCR activation.
source: Thus, within a physiological stiffness range, T cells scan their substrate through thin protrusions but do not spread extensively their cell body in response to TCR activation
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental observations from scanning electron microscopy.

claim: The main differences in gene expression were observed between the conditions with/without aCD3.
source: This analysis revealed that the main differences in gene expression were observed between the conditions with/without aCD3.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effect of substrate stiffness on T cell gene expression was mainly observed when the TCR/CD3 was stimulated.
source: Moreover, the effect of substrate stiffness on T cell gene expression was mainly observed when the TCR/CD3 was stimulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The number of genes with significantly changed expression was very low for T cells on the soft 0.5 kPa gel (34 up-regulated and seven down-regulated).
source: The number of genes with significantly changed expression was very low for T cells on the soft 0.5 kPa gel (34 up-regulated and seven down-regulated) and increased on the stiffer 6.4 kPa (2007 up and 1011 down) and 100 kPa gels (2611 up and 1744 down) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The number of genes with significantly changed expression increased on the stiffer 6.4 kPa (2007 up and 1011 down) and 100 kPa gels (2611 up and 1744 down).
source: The number of genes with significantly changed expression was very low for T cells on the soft 0.5 kPa gel (34 up-regulated and seven down-regulated) and increased on the stiffer 6.4 kPa (2007 up and 1011 down) and 100 kPa gels (2611 up and 1744 down) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The TCR/CD3 is the main rigidity sensing receptor.
source: This suggests that the TCR/CD3 is herein the main rigidity sensing receptor and that it induces stronger signaling when its ligand is attached to stiff rather than soft substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that gene expression changes are mainly observed in the presence of aCD3 stimulation.

claim: The TCR induces stronger signaling when its ligand is attached to stiff rather than soft substrates.
source: This suggests that the TCR/CD3 is herein the main rigidity sensing receptor and that it induces stronger signaling when its ligand is attached to stiff rather than soft substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that more genes are differentially expressed on stiffer substrates in the presence of aCD3.

claim: Cytokines (TNF, IFNG, LTA, IL22, IL17A) show enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3.
source: Cytokines (TNF, IFNG, LTA, IL22, IL17A), T cell surface markers (BTLA, IL4R, CD40LG, IL2RA, CD69, ICOS), T-cell-specific transcription factors (TBX21 and FOXP3) and the proliferation transcription factor MYC all showed enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: T cell surface markers (BTLA, IL4R, CD40LG, IL2RA, CD69, ICOS) show enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3.
source: Cytokines (TNF, IFNG, LTA, IL22, IL17A), T cell surface markers (BTLA, IL4R, CD40LG, IL2RA, CD69, ICOS), T-cell-specific transcription factors (TBX21 and FOXP3) and the proliferation transcription factor MYC all showed enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: T-cell-specific transcription factors (TBX21 and FOXP3) show enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3.
source: Cytokines (TNF, IFNG, LTA, IL22, IL17A), T cell surface markers (BTLA, IL4R, CD40LG, IL2RA, CD69, ICOS), T-cell-specific transcription factors (TBX21 and FOXP3) and the proliferation transcription factor MYC all showed enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The proliferation transcription factor MYC shows enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3.
source: Cytokines (TNF, IFNG, LTA, IL22, IL17A), T cell surface markers (BTLA, IL4R, CD40LG, IL2RA, CD69, ICOS), T-cell-specific transcription factors (TBX21 and FOXP3) and the proliferation transcription factor MYC all showed enhanced gene expression with increasing stiffness in the presence of aCD3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gene expression of the translation initiation factor EIF4E is increased in response to stiffness.
source: Gene expression of the translation initiation factor EIF4E, which is up-regulated with T cell activation (Bjur et al., 2013), and the metabolic regulator for promoting glycolysis HIF1A (Pollizzi and Powell, 2014) was also increased in response to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data and citations to previous research (Bjur et al., 2013).

claim: Gene expression of the metabolic regulator for promoting glycolysis HIF1A is increased in response to stiffness.
source: Gene expression of the translation initiation factor EIF4E, which is up-regulated with T cell activation (Bjur et al., 2013), and the metabolic regulator for promoting glycolysis HIF1A (Pollizzi and Powell, 2014) was also increased in response to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data and citations to previous research (Pollizzi and Powell, 2014).

claim: Expression of lamin genes (LMNA, LMNB1, LMNB2) is gradually increased with stiffness on aCD3-coated PA-gels.
source: Of note, expression of lamin genes (LMNA, LMNB1, LMNB2), which has been shown for other cell types to scale with tissue stiffness (Swift et al., 2013), was gradually increased with stiffness on aCD3-coated PA-gels (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to previous research (Swift et al., 2013).

claim: TCR induced gene expression is potentiated by the stiffness of the surface presenting TCR ligands.
source: Overall, these results show that TCR induced gene expression is potentiated by the stiffness of the surface presenting TCR ligands and genes related to CD4+ T cell immune response are particularly sensitive.
evidence: The claim is supported by the microarray data showing increased gene expression with increasing stiffness.

claim: Genes related to CD4+ T cell immune response are particularly sensitive to stiffness.
source: Overall, these results show that TCR induced gene expression is potentiated by the stiffness of the surface presenting TCR ligands and genes related to CD4+ T cell immune response are particularly sensitive.
evidence: The claim is supported by the microarray data showing enhanced expression of immune-related genes with increasing stiffness.

claim: Most of the enriched gene sets are common for the three different substrates and include cell-cycle-related and immune-response-related processes.
source: Results showed that most of the enriched gene sets were common for the three different substrates and these included cell-cycle-related and immune-response-related processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The stiff 100 kPa gel causes the enrichment of a higher number of gene sets in response to aCD3 stimulation.
source: The stiff 100 kPa gel caused the enrichment of a higher number of gene sets in response to aCD3 stimulation, due to specific enrichment of gene sets such as mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The 6.4 and 100 kPa PA-gels induce mostly common pathways, which are mitotic cell cycle, transcription and translation related.
source: Pathway analysis on the differentially up-regulated genes, using the GO and the KEGG databases, showed that the 6.4 and 100 kPa PA-gels induced mostly common pathways, which were mitotic cell cycle, transcription and translation related (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 3, 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary files 3, 4.

claim: For the 0.5 kPa PA-gel, the two most prominent pathways induced are T cell activation and differentiation.
source: For the 0.5 kPa PA-gel, the two most prominent pathways induced were T cell activation and differentiation (Figure 3B), showing that the TCR was responsive from the softest end of the stiffness range.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The TCR is responsive from the softest end of the stiffness range.
source: For the 0.5 kPa PA-gel, the two most prominent pathways induced were T cell activation and differentiation (Figure 3B), showing that the TCR was responsive from the softest end of the stiffness range.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T cell activation and differentiation pathways are induced even at 0.5 kPa.

claim: The two most prominent pathways induced only on the 100 kPa gels include respiratory electron transport and translation-related pathways.
source: The two most prominent pathways induced only on the 100 kPa gels included respiratory electron transport (e.g. genes of ATP synthase) and translation-related pathways (ribosomal protein genes) (Figure 3B, Supplementary files 3, 4), showing that induction of these pathways required the stronger signaling provided by TCR ligands on the stiff substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary files 3, 4.

claim: Induction of respiratory electron transport and translation-related pathways requires the stronger signaling provided by TCR ligands on the stiff substrate.
source: The two most prominent pathways induced only on the 100 kPa gels included respiratory electron transport (e.g. genes of ATP synthase) and translation-related pathways (ribosomal protein genes) (Figure 3B, Supplementary files 3, 4), showing that induction of these pathways required the stronger signaling provided by TCR ligands on the stiff substrate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these pathways are only enriched at 100 kPa.

claim: K-means hierarchical clustering identified three major clusters: one with strong up-regulation (containing 1022 probes), one with weak down-regulation (containing 4412 probes) and one with weak or no up-regulation (containing 5928 probes).
source: Three major clusters were identified (Figure 3C): one with strong up-regulation (containing 1022 probes), one with weak down-regulation (containing 4412 probes) and one with weak or no up-regulation (containing 5928 probes).
evidence: The claim is supported by K-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pathway analysis of the strongly up-regulated cluster demonstrates enrichment of mostly cell cycle processes, cytokine signaling, nucleotide biosynthesis and ribosomal biogenesis.
source: Pathway analysis of the strongly up-regulated cluster demonstrated enrichment of mostly cell cycle processes, cytokine signaling, nucleotide biosynthesis and ribosomal biogenesis (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The strongly up-regulated cluster shows a response to aCD3 that gradually increases with stiffness.
source: The strongly up-regulated cluster showed a response to aCD3 that gradually increased with stiffness.
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis and visualization of gene expression patterns.

claim: The majority of the genes in the strongly up-regulated cluster show expression that is more increased from 0.5 kPa to 6.4 kPa than from 6.4 kPa to 100 kPa.
source: The majority of the genes showed an expression that was more increased from 0.5 kPa to 6.4 kPa (right of the diagonal) than from 6.4 kPa to 100 kPa (left of the diagonal) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Many genes show expression that continues to rise for both transitions (genes close to the diagonal), such as IL4R, CD69, NFKBIB, ENO1, PGK1, LMNA, and LMNB1.
source: Many genes showed expression that continued to rise for both transitions (genes close to the diagonal), such as IL4R, CD69, NFKBIB, ENO1, PGK1, LMNA, and LMNB1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of genes involved in the main TCR/CD3 induced T cell functions is sensitive to stiffness.
source: The results from these three analyses show that expression of genes involved in the main TCR/CD3 induced T cell functions is sensitive to stiffness, with some functions (cytokine signaling, T cell activation) being induced in the low range of stiffness values and others (respiratory electron transport and glycolysis) requiring higher stiffness to be induced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression and pathway analyses.

claim: Some functions (cytokine signaling, T cell activation) are induced in the low range of stiffness values.
source: The results from these three analyses show that expression of genes involved in the main TCR/CD3 induced T cell functions is sensitive to stiffness, with some functions (cytokine signaling, T cell activation) being induced in the low range of stiffness values and others (respiratory electron transport and glycolysis) requiring higher stiffness to be induced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression and pathway analyses.

claim: Other functions (respiratory electron transport and glycolysis) require higher stiffness to be induced.
source: The results from these three analyses show that expression of genes involved in the main TCR/CD3 induced T cell functions is sensitive to stiffness, with some functions (cytokine signaling, T cell activation) being induced in the low range of stiffness values and others (respiratory electron transport and glycolysis) requiring higher stiffness to be induced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression and pathway analyses.

claim: Cytokine production shows a graded response to stiffness in the presence of aCD3.
source: Cytokine production showed a graded response to stiffness in the presence of aCD3 (Figure 4A and B) confirming the results obtained on gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements of IFNγ and TNFα shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: A similar potentiating effect of stiffness on cytokine production is observed when ten times lower amount of aCD3 is used.
source: A similar potentiating effect of stiffness was observed when ten times lower amount of aCD3 was used (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD25 expression is only increased when T cells are activated on the aCD3+aCD28+ICAM-1-coated stiff 100 kPa gels.
source: In contrast, CD25 expression, which was already present on the surface of T lymphoblasts, was only increased when T cells were activated on the aCD3+aCD28+ICAM-1-coated stiff 100 kPa gels (Figure 4C and D), whereas its gene expression was increased from 0.5 kPa (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Stiffness sensing by T cells requires physical interaction of the TCR/CD3 complex to the gel substrate.
source: We then sought to confirm whether stiffness sensing by T cells required physical interaction of the TCR/CD3 complex to the gel substrate. CD4+ T lymphoblasts were cultured on PA-gels of varying stiffness coated with ICAM-1 and soluble aCD3+aCD28 were added. In these conditions, IFNγ production was not affected by gel stiffness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing that mechanosensing indeed requires direct engagement of the TCR/CD3 complex with ligands on substrates of varying stiffness.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that soluble aCD3 does not result in stiffness-dependent cytokine production (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: ICAM-1 is not essential for the stiffness-mediated modulation of cytokine production.
source: Moreover, in the absence of ICAM-1 (PA-gels coated solely with biotinylated aCD3+aCD28), production of cytokines still followed substrate stiffness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) showing that ICAM-1 is not essential for the stiffness-mediated modulation of cytokine production.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing cytokine production follows stiffness even without ICAM-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Freshly isolated memory CD4+ T cells show increased production of cytokines (IFNγ and IL-2) and increased expression of the activation marker CD69 in response to increasing stiffness.
source: These results were confirmed on freshly isolated memory CD4+ T cells, which also showed increased production of cytokines (IFNγ and IL-2) and increased expression of the activation marker CD69 in response to increasing stiffness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on memory CD4+ T cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TCR/CD3-induced cytokine production by effector and memory human CD4+ T cells is increased by the rigidity of substrates bearing TCR ligands.
source: Overall, our results show that TCR/CD3-induced cytokine production by effector and memory human CD4+ T cells is increased by the rigidity of substrates bearing TCR ligands and shows exquisite sensitivity within the physiological range of cellular (0.5 and 6.4 kPa) and tissue rigidity (100 kPa).
evidence: The claim is supported by the cytokine production data from both effector and memory T cells.

claim: TCR/CD3-induced cytokine production shows exquisite sensitivity within the physiological range of cellular (0.5 and 6.4 kPa) and tissue rigidity (100 kPa).
source: Overall, our results show that TCR/CD3-induced cytokine production by effector and memory human CD4+ T cells is increased by the rigidity of substrates bearing TCR ligands and shows exquisite sensitivity within the physiological range of cellular (0.5 and 6.4 kPa) and tissue rigidity (100 kPa).
evidence: The claim is supported by the cytokine production data across the range of stiffness values tested.

claim: The presence of aCD3 on PA-gels induces more lactate production by T cells than aCD28+ICAM1 alone.
source: The presence of aCD3 on PA-gels induced more lactate production by T cells than aCD28+ICAM1 alone (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: After 24 hr, lactate production is significantly higher in the presence of aCD3, similar when cells are activated on 0.5 and 6.4 kPa PA-gels and more pronounced on the stiff 100 kPa PA-gel.
source: After 24 hr, lactate production was significantly higher in the presence of aCD3, similar when cells were activated on 0.5 and 6.4 kPa PA-gels and more pronounced on the stiff 100 kPa PA-gel (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The T cell glycolytic switch induced by TCR triggering is increased by high stiffness values (100 kPa) but not by low ones (hundreds to thousands of Pa).
source: These results show that the T cell glycolytic switch induced by TCR triggering was increased by high stiffness values (100 kPa) but not by low ones (hundreds to thousands of Pa).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lactate production data showing significant increase only at 100 kPa.

claim: The percentage of phospho-rpS6+ T cells does not show any increase when rigidity goes from 0.5 to 6.4 kPa, but is significantly increased for substrate of 100 kPa.
source: Also, the percentage of phospho-rpS6+ T cells did not show any increase when rigidity went from 0.5 to 6.4 kPa, but was significantly increased for substrate of 100 kPa (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both glycolytic capacity and maximal mitochondrial respiratory capacity demonstrate a potentiation with stiffness after 48 hr of culture.
source: While, at 24 hr no clear differences were observed in the glycolytic capacity and maximal respiration of T cells activated on varying stiffness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), both parameters demonstrated a potentiation with stiffness after 48 hr of culture (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse metabolic assay data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: At 24 hr, cell cycle progression is only evident for T cells activated by aCD3 on the high end of the stiffness range (100 kPa).
source: Results revealed that, at 24 hr, cell cycle progression, that is fewer cells in G0/G1 phases and significantly more cells in S phase and G2/M phases, was only evident for T cells activated by aCD3 on the high end of the stiffness range (100 kPa) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After 72 hr of culture, cell cycle progression is induced by aCD3 within the whole stiffness range tested.
source: After 72 hr of culture, cell cycle progression was induced by aCD3 within the whole stiffness range tested (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TCR/CD3-induced proliferation of T cells demonstrates a graded response to stiffness at 72 hr.
source: Finally, TCR/CD3-induced proliferation of T cells was measured at 72 hr, demonstrating a graded response to stiffness (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In 24 hr, varying stiffness within the range measured for APCs (hundreds to thousands of Pa) does not modulate T cell metabolism or cell cycle progression induced by low density of activating molecules.
source: Altogether, these results show that, in 24 hr, varying stiffness within the range measured for APCs (hundreds to thousands of Pa) does not modulate T cell metabolism or cell cycle progression induced by low density of activating molecules (our conditions herein).
evidence: The claim is supported by the metabolic and cell cycle data at 24 hr.

claim: Metabolism and cell cycle progression are increased by high stiffness (100 kPa), observed for tissue, extracellular matrix or tumoral environment.
source: Instead, metabolism and cell cycle progression are increased by high stiffness (100 kPa), observed for tissue, extracellular matrix or tumoral environment (Paszek et al., 2005; Cox and Erler, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by the metabolic and cell cycle data at 24 hr and citations to previous research (Paszek et al., 2005; Cox and Erler, 2011).

claim: T cell response to stiffness builds on with time, resulting eventually in a potentiation of T cell proliferation within the whole stiffness range tested.
source: These results also show that T cell response to stiffness builds on with time, resulting eventually in a potentiation of T cell proliferation within the whole stiffness range tested.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of responses at different time points.

claim: HeLa-CIITA cells show more spreading on 28 kPa gels (569 ± 25 μm2) than on 1.5 kPa gels (453 ± 14 μm2).
source: HeLa-CIITA cells showed more spreading on 28 kPa gels (569 ± 25 μm2, ncells: 215) than on 1.5 kPa gels (453 ± 14 μm2, ncells: 254) (Figure 7A and B), showing adaptation to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell area measurements shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: HeLa-CIITA cells adapt to stiffness.
source: HeLa-CIITA cells showed more spreading on 28 kPa gels (569 ± 25 μm2, ncells: 215) than on 1.5 kPa gels (453 ± 14 μm2, ncells: 254) (Figure 7A and B), showing adaptation to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HeLa-CIITA cells spread more on stiffer substrates.

claim: The Young's modulus of HeLa-CIITA cells is 1.72 ± 0.2 kPa on 28 kPa PDMS and 1.43 ± 0.15 kPa on 1.5 kPa PDMS.
source: Although the differences in HeLa-CIITA cell rigidity on the two different PDMS substrates were not significant, the tendency was for a higher Young's modulus for cells plated on the stiffer substrate: 1.72 ± 0.2 kPa (ncells: 15) on 28 kPa versus 1.43 ± 0.15 kPa (ncells: 13) on 1.5 kPa (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Young's modulus measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: HeLa cells modulate their Young's modulus weakly with substrate rigidity as compared to fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem cells.
source: While these values for HeLa cells are in excellent agreement with previous AFM measurements (Shimizu et al., 2012), they reveal that HeLa cells modulated their Young's modulus weakly with substrate rigidity as compared to fibroblasts (Solon et al., 2007) and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) (Tee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature (Shimizu et al., 2012; Solon et al., 2007; Tee et al., 2011).

claim: Addition of TSST1 induces a dose-dependent increase of cytokine production that is higher when the HeLa-CIITA APCs are plated on the stiffer 28 kPa gel than on the softer 1.5 kPa gel.
source: Addition of TSST1 induced a dose-dependent increase of cytokine production that was higher when the HeLa-CIITA APCs were plated on the stiffer 28 kPa gel than on the softer 1.5 kPa gel.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements of IFNγ and TNFα in co-culture experiments shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: T lymphocytes are submitted to the small variation of mechanical properties of the HeLa-CIITA monolayers (~ hundreds of Pa) in the co-culture setting.
source: It is worth noting that, in the co-culture setting, T lymphocytes were not submitted to the stiffness range of the PDMS gels (1.5 to 28 kPa) but rather to the small variation of mechanical properties of the HeLa-CIITA monolayers (~ hundreds of Pa), suggesting that cytokine production by T lymphocytes is exquisitely sensitive to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Young's modulus measurements of HeLa-CIITA cells.

claim: Cytokine production by T lymphocytes is exquisitely sensitive to stiffness.
source: It is worth noting that, in the co-culture setting, T lymphocytes were not submitted to the stiffness range of the PDMS gels (1.5 to 28 kPa) but rather to the small variation of mechanical properties of the HeLa-CIITA monolayers (~ hundreds of Pa), suggesting that cytokine production by T lymphocytes is exquisitely sensitive to stiffness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small differences in APC stiffness affect cytokine production.

claim: T cell activation by adherent APCs plated on substrates of varying stiffness follows the same rules as activation on artificial substrates.
source: These results demonstrate that T cell activation by adherent APCs plated on substrates of varying stiffness follows the same rules as activation on artificial substrates, that is cytokine production is enhanced by increasing stiffness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of results from PA-gel experiments and co-culture experiments.

claim: TCR mechanosensitivity occurs when T cells are activated with the superantigen TSST1.
source: Moreover, we find that TCR mechanosensitivity also occurs when T cells are activated with the superantigen TSST1, showing that this sensitivity is not induced only by aCD3.
evidence: The claim is supported by the co-culture experiments using TSST1.

claim: APC mechanical properties can be an important physiological parameter contributing to antigen-induced cytokine production by CD4+ T cells.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that APC mechanical properties can be an important physiological parameter contributing to antigen-induced cytokine production by CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-culture experiments showing that APC stiffness affects T cell cytokine production.

claim: Stiffness influences in a rheostat-like fashion many aspects of CD4+ T cell response, including spreading, stop signal, transcription of several genes, cytokine production, metabolism and cell cycle progression.
source: Overall, our data reveal that stiffness influences in a rheostat-like fashion many aspects of CD4+ T cell response, that is spreading, stop signal, transcription of several genes, cytokine production, metabolism and cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TCR itself has been shown to act as a mechanosensor.
source: the T cell receptor (TCR) itself has been shown to act as a mechanosensor (Kim et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kim et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010).

claim: T cells generate forces upon activation and costimulation.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bashour et al., 2014; Hu and Butte, 2016; Husson et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016).

claim: T cells adapt to the stiffening of an artificial APC by changing the loading rate of their pulling forces.
source: T cells were also found to adapt to the stiffening of an artificial APC by changing the loading rate of their pulling forces (Husson et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Husson et al., 2011).

claim: The surface density of aCD3 was calculated to be in the range of 2 to 4 molecules/μm2.
source: The surface density of aCD3 was calculated to be in the range of 2 to 4 molecules/μm2, that is in the low range of agonist densities used in other studies (Grakoui et al., 1999; Krummel et al., 2000; Purtic et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from experimental parameters and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The calculated aCD3 density roughly corresponds to 100 to 1000 MHC-peptides per APC.
source: It roughly corresponded to 100 to 1000 MHC-peptides per APC, close to the minimum number of pMHC complexes reported to induce cytokine production by T cells (Harding and Unanue, 1990; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations and comparison with cited literature (Harding and Unanue, 1990; Huang et al., 2013).

claim: ICAM-1-Fc density was calculated to be in the range of 20 to 40 molecules/μm2.

claim: The stiffness of substrates bearing TCR ligands can act as a modulator of TCR ligand avidity.
source: We propose that the stiffness of substrates bearing TCR ligands can act as a modulator of TCR ligand avidity.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and established knowledge about catch bonds.

claim: Forces exerted on agonist pMHC/TCR bonds prolong lifetimes of these bonds (catch bond effect).
source: Indeed, forces exerted on agonist pMHC/TCR bonds were shown to prolong lifetimes of these bonds; this has been called the catch bond effect (Liu et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Liu et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2015).

claim: Stiffness modulates the forces developed by T cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Husson et al., 2011; Bashour et al., 2014).

claim: Increased forces developed by CD4+ T cells on the TCR/ligand bonds present on stiff substrates should increase avidity of the bonds, leading to potentiation of TCR/CD3-induced activation of T cells.
source: Thus, increased forces developed by CD4+ T cells on the TCR/ligand bonds present on stiff substrates should increase avidity of the bonds, leading to potentiation of TCR/CD3-induced activation of T cells.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and established knowledge about catch bonds and force generation.

claim: The physiological parameters promoting TCR-induced T cell responses include not only the number of ligands and the TCR affinity for ligand, but also the stiffness of the surface presenting the ligands.
source: Therefore, our findings show that the physiological parameters promoting TCR-induced T cell responses include not only the number of ligands and the TCR affinity for ligand, but also the stiffness of the surface presenting the ligands.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Lamins control cell trafficking and differentiation of hematopoietic cell types.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Shin et al., 2013; González-Granado et al., 2014).

claim: Lamins control T cell activation.

claim: Substrate stiffness should be considered for the optimal expansion of T cells used in applications such as cancer immunotherapy.
